doc.title: Ruth Brown interviewed by Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995

title: Radio disc jockeys and hiding the radio from parents
summary: Brown talks about DJs spreading the music, kids hiding radios, and secretly tuning in 'The Mail Bag' at home.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: And the music was really trying to send a message wasn’t it?

And the music was, at that time. You see people had control over where you could go, where you could sit, but the one thing about that music was that it was the radio, the disc jockeys who played that music who were responsible for the music becoming what it was. And parents, unlike today with television I think and changed channels, they had no control over the radio dial, you see? And I’ve had many kids come to me and say they had to hide their radio, put the pillow over it, anything so the parents wouldn’t know what was playing. But they could turn that dial and hear what was being done, and enjoyed it. And having to listen to a radio DJ, now unlike seeing everything visual on television, you had to use your imagination a little bit. And we had disc jockeys that were just funny, clean, funny and creative. They all had a character of their own, you know they had a slang talk, a way of speaking that, even myself in the beginning I’d get up and as soon as

my daddy was out the house and I could see him going to work, I would switch the dial to a radio station that played a program “The Mail Bag.” My daddy didn’t want us to hear it in the house. But as soon as he was out, you know, that’s where we would turn it, to “The Mail Bag.” So radio was very very important in that particular time. The DJs, you’d get into town and you’d have to go in to these radio stations and talk, and a lot of times people would not buy tickets because you bought tickets at the door. There was not all that much advanced sale. What was done in advance was when the posters went up that you were coming into town. Those posters usually went up at least a month before you got there.
